blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A colleague builds tie-break weights from Python's hash() of each project id and checks that they repeat by solving twice in one Python session. What happens after the service restarts?

options.text: The weights repeat, since a string's hash depends on its text alone
options.says: The printed ranks of the same ids differ between two processes with different hash seeds.

options.text: The weights repeat, since the solver's seed fixes Python's hashes too
options.says: A solver seed has nothing to do with Python's string hashing, which is salted per process.

options.text: The weights may change, since each process salts its string hashes
options.says: Right: one session repeats, a new process does not; use a hashlib digest or the sorted index.

options.text: The weights may change, since sha256 digests are salted per process too
options.says: The printed sha256 ranks are the same in both processes; only the hash() ranks change.

origin.section: Trap Questions: Settings That Do Not Do What They Promise

questions.stem: A CP-SAT service sets num_workers = 8, a fixed random seed and a deterministic limit. Does a rerun of the same snapshot return the same plan?

options.text: Yes, since a fixed seed makes the eight workers repeat their search
options.says: Eight workers with a seed under a deterministic limit gave different plans in lesson 4.6.3.

options.text: Yes, since eight workers with a seed is the deterministic parallel mode
options.says: That is the study-guide claim the trap corrects; the workers still race.

options.text: No, since CP-SAT repeats a plan just when a time limit is also set
options.says: A clock limit makes repeats less likely; one worker with a seed and a deterministic limit repeated.

options.text: Not reliably, since the workers race unless the search is interleaved
options.says: Right: only interleave_search, or one worker with a seed and a deterministic limit, repeated.

origin.section: Trap Questions: Settings That Do Not Do What They Promise

questions.stem: A nightly job solves a large transportation LP with cuOpt, leaving every setting as shipped. Two runs of one snapshot report objectives a few parts in 100,000 apart. What explains it?

options.text: GPU arithmetic is random, so two GPU solves of one LP seldom repeat
options.says: cuOpt's PDLP and HiGHS's GPU PDLP each repeated bit for bit in every run measured.

options.text: Several LP methods race in each solve, and any of them may answer first
options.says: Right: cuOpt's default LP method is concurrent; set the method to PDLP and state the tolerance.

options.text: PDLP answered both runs, and its answers drift between repeated runs
options.says: cuOpt's PDLP repeated bit for bit in every run measured; the drift comes from the concurrent method, where a different method can answer each run.

options.text: PDLP ends at a vertex, and two vertices tied within the tolerance
options.says: PDLP stops when its errors fall below a tolerance, not at an exact vertex.

origin.section: Round 3: A GPU Speeds Up Large LPs, and the Run Says Which Device Answered

questions.stem: In the start-year model, a planner says 'fund P4, in any year of its window'. How is that put into the model?

options.text: As one labelled row: the sum of P4's start variables equals one
options.says: Right: it is a sum over years, so no single bound can say it.

options.text: As a lower bound of one on P4's start variable in its first year
options.says: That forces the first year, a start-in override, not 'any year'.

options.text: As a lower bound of one on each one of P4's start variables
options.says: With the once row, that makes the model infeasible whenever P4 has two or more years.

options.text: As an upper bound of zero on P4's start variables outside the plan
options.says: Variables outside the window do not exist; bounds of zero forbid starts, they never fund one.
